## Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes

- ch. 1 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The editor's introduction argues that Adventure Time is philosophy in disguise: its theme-song promise of 'very distant lands' describes the philosopher's trek into unpopular, even hated ideas, and the show treats 'crazy' questions as fun rather than frightening. It names the questions the book will chase—whether Finn was fated to lose his arm, whether the Ice King is really a bad guy, what evil really means—and claims that since common sense has always turned out to be wrong (matter isn't solid, the Earth moves), the childlike willingness to reconsider everything is a philosophical virtue. Philosophy, like the show, is an adventure best taken with a friend.
- ch. 8 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Karl Popper — Falsificationism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Karavitis argues Finn's 'Finn-losophy' is a metaphysics that prefers magic over Princess Bubblegum's science, and that this choice shapes his ethics: magic is the 'easy way out' requiring no understanding (Jake's stretching, the Glasses of Nerdicon), while science demands observation, experiment, and falsifiable ideas—'reality is the ultimate spell-checker.' Because magic promises instant gratification, Finn rushes into danger ('Wizard,' 'Donny,' the Goblin Kingdom) behind an inflexible hero code, and his altruism misfires, as the never-ending prize-winning battles of the 'Mystery Train' episode illustrate. The chapter concludes that your view of how the world works—magical or scientific—determines whether you can grow ethically at all.
- ch. 10 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger — The Question Concerning Technology — Leonard reads Ooo through Heidegger's contrast between technological and poetic frames of mind: Princess Bubblegum's BGCCTV, Goliad, and the James clone mission treat candy people as manipulable stock, while the Lich is technological thinking perfected—pure efficiency aimed at 'the extinction of all life'—and Finn is the poet who values things for what they are, risks Heidegger's 'venture,' and battles Death in 'Death in Bloom' as if in a concert. On Heidegger's definition of art as 'the setting-itself-into-work of truth,' Marceline's songs and Jake's imagined lava show creation disclosing reality. Magic, spread by the Mushroom War, sits between the two modes, and only Finn's poetic exuberance can check Bubblegum's slide toward order at any cost.
- ch. 11 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes — The Social Contract — Caballeros argues that political legitimacy in Ooo runs through parenthood: Princess Bubblegum rules the citizens she created ('You made me... you are my Glob'), the Ice King is redeemed when we learn Simon protected child Marceline, and the Flame King and Hunson Abadeer forfeit standing as fathers. Using Hobbes's view that a ruler is legitimate insofar as he protects his subjects, the chapter asks whether Bubblegum's protection-cum-manipulation—sabotaging Finn to let James die, jailing Tree Trunks—still counts, and it contrasts justified rebellion (Flame Princess deposing her father, Marceline resisting Abadeer) with Lumpy Space Princess's disastrous one. Good parenting, like good government, earns obedience; bad parenting loses the crown.
- ch. 12 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; Natural Rights; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — Gale and Barkman treat post-Mushroom-War Ooo as a state-of-nature laboratory for liberalism's three founders. The Forest Wizard who cages Finn in 'Storytelling' is Hobbes's Leviathan, kept in power by fear yet moderated by self-interest (Goblin King Xergiok's fall shows the leash); Princess Bubblegum's Candy Kingdom is Locke's civil society where citizens trade private revenge for impartial law—her lawful bow to Lemongrab shows she rules by contract, not fear; and 'City of Thieves' illustrates Rousseau's claim that property corrupts natural goodness, with Finn and Jake as his uncorrupted natural people. The chapter concludes that the rights language these thinkers forged is what keeps both Ooo and our world from sliding back into a war of all against all.
- ch. 13 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Aquinas — Doctrine of Double Effect; The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism; The Drowning Child (obligation to aid) — Montoya tests Simon's choice to sacrifice his sanity by wearing the crown to save child Marceline against three ethical theories. Aquinas's doctrine of double effect clears him because the intended good (saving her life) outweighs the merely foreseen side effect (her tears, his possible future evils); Kant's categorical imperative rules out universalizing 'let children die to save myself,' since a world of universal using destroys the rule itself; and a fountain case where Finn must choose between world-saving plans and a drowning candy child separates act from rule utilitarianism, with rule utilitarianism preserving the duty to rescue. All three converge on the verdict that Simon, not Finn, is Ooo's greatest hero.
- ch. 14 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Forgiveness; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Moral Luck — McCrossin asks why Finn and Jake forgive Marceline although she tries to kill Jake, evicts them twice, drains Princess Bubblegum, and never shows remorse. Jake's change of heart ('my fear was based on ignorance') comes from witnessing her father Hunson Abadeer's cruelty and her abandoned childhood, so her bad acts flow from causes outside her control rather than pure choice. The chapter presses the remaining problem: we normally forgive the penitent offender, not the unrepentant one, and Marceline—unlike the moping vampires of Twilight, Underworld, and True Blood—never regrets, leaving readers to decide whether understanding without remorse can ground trust and friendship.
- ch. 15 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** David Hume — Problem of Induction; Philosophical Skepticism — Michaud plays the 'David Hume' Card Wars deck against Princess Bubblegum's confidence in science: following Hume's problem of induction, every scientific law rests on observation and is only probabilistic—we never observe the necessary connection between cause and effect, whether in magnetism, Jake's hunger-induced jerkiness, or the first law of thermodynamics. Humans are pattern-makers who project causal order onto the world (seeing Gunter in clouds, blaming one bubblegum incident), while quantum physics reveals genuine randomness that Einstein hated. Ooo's residents, who watch Tree Trunks explode and simply move on, may grasp reality better than we do, because they never smuggle in stable, lawlike expectations that the show—and the universe—keep violating.
- ch. 17 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Littmann uses Adventure Time as a stockpile of thought experiments against free will: Finn excuses Billy (possessed by the Lich), hug-wolf Finn, amulet-Marceline, red-starved Marceline, the magically animated hat Little Dude, and crown-cursed Simon, yet punishes the Lich and Lemongrab, whose destructive desires are exactly as unchosen—Lemongrab even protests 'you made me like this.' Since deterministic causation and randomness exhaust the options, we are 'machines made of meat' wearing ice crowns inside our skulls, so deserved suffering makes no sense. The chapter concludes that just-deserts retribution (Princess Cookie's life sentence, America's prisons) should give way to deterrence, protection, and rehabilitation—freeing the Simon Petrikovs underneath.
- ch. 18 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Free Will vs Determinism; Fate and Foreknowledge; Compatibilism — Miller argues from Jake's croak dream, the Cosmic Owl, and the Dungeon Train's future crystal that Ooo's future is real, visible, and changeable—hence a case of soft determinism: the dream of Jake dying in space is what caused Finn to accompany him and avert it, so the only being who could have intended the change, the Owl, is the sole certain free agent in Ooo. Every alternate Finn is missing his right arm—Shoko the thief, Farmworld Finn, pillow-world Finn, the Dungeon Train elder—hinting at an epic destiny, yet Finn altered the train future once he saw where it led Jake. The chapter closes on the open question of whether choosing one's fate differs from having it thrust on one, since every choice is caused by the past no one can change.
- ch. 19 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Gottfried Leibniz — The Best of All Possible Worlds; The Problem of Evil; Possible Worlds — Montoya asks whether Prismo, Adventure Time's wish-granting stand-in for God, produced the best possible world when he restored Ooo over Farmworld. After explaining Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil—that an all-good, all-knowing God permits some evil because every possible world contains some, and ours contains the least—the chapter compares Farmworld (no Lich, but Finn becomes the Ice King, Jake mutates into the Lich, Marceline dies ancient and insane) with Ooo, where the same characters flourish as heroes. Prismo, no omnibenevolent deity, remakes Ooo out of friendship with Jake, and Farmworld's horrors vindicate the Leibnizian point that wishing one evil out of existence can unleash far worse.
- ch. 20 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Death of God; Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura) — Namvol argues that 'Glob' is the post-apocalyptic corpse of the Christian God: combining Don Cupitt's claim that gods live only in worship and practice with Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' he traces how the Mushroom War destroyed the believers, churches, and rituals that kept God alive, leaving Ooo an empty exclamation. Pantheism fails as a rescue because evil is native to Ooo's nature (Gunter, the eternally self-existing Abadeer), so God cannot simply have become the land. Against Dostoevsky's 'without God all things are permitted,' the chapter sides with Žižek—that morality's shadow, guilt, outlives God—as when Finn's self-regulation kicks in after 'All the Little People' and 'Dungeon Train,' making Finn, not Glob, the true savior of a godless world.
- ch. 21 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Muniz uses the 'Ocean of Fear' material to stage the paradox of fiction—we know Finn, Jake, and the Lich are drawings, yet we genuinely fear for the child hero in danger—and works through its three sentences: we respond emotionally only to what we believe real, we disbelieve fiction, yet we respond to fiction constantly. Distinguishing passive startle from active dwelling, he tests escape routes: fear at Marceline's abandonment may really be fear for our own children, the robot attack in 'Business Men' may become 'real' to a viewer, and some philosophers call our responses mere 'fictional emotions.' Finding no sentence safely deniable, he concludes that our emotional responses to Adventure Time are, strictly speaking, irrational—but no less honest for it.
- ch. 23 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Jones reads Adventure Time through Gadamer's account of play in Truth and Method: play is the 'mode of being' of the artwork, and Finn's all-in commitment—the 'sacred seriousness' that makes a spoilsport of anyone who mocks the rules, as in 'Slumber Party Panic' or Finn's bloodlust in 'Morituri Te Salutamus'—is why the show counts as art. The finished episode is Gadamer's 'transformation into structure,' and like a festival or a favorite board game it exists in its return, episode after episode. Interpreting the show is itself play: holding our world and Ooo's world in two palms brought together is Gadamer's fusion of horizons, through which Finn corrects our concepts of a boy or a hero and makes new understanding, even empathy, possible.
- ch. 24 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Plato, David Hume, George Berkeley — Allegory of the Cave; Subjective Idealism (esse est percipi); Bundle Theory of Self; Philosophical Skepticism — Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.
- ch. 25 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** J.M.E. McTaggart, Henri Bergson, David Lewis — The A-Series and B-Series of Time; Duration (durée); Possible Worlds — Through a hot-tub dialogue in Prismo's Time Room, the chapter walks Jake through the main theories of time: McTaggart's A-theory versus B-theory, plus presentism, the growing block, eternalism and four-dimensionalism, illustrated with the mirror-Finn dream, Farmworld Finn, Jake's unchangeable croak dream, and the Ancient Psychic Tandem War Elephant as a thing stretched across past, present and future selves. Booko's description of the multiverse becomes a springboard for David Lewis's possible-worlds realism and Everett's many-worlds reading of Prismo's 'alternate wish worlds'. Finally, quotes from McTaggart and Bergson delivered as Finn's Glasses of Nerdicon rant argue that time resists spatial and scientific analysis and must be lived, which the authors tie to relativity, black-hole cosmology and Prismo's Time Room as the one dimension outside time.
- ch. 26 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Sigmund Freud, Michel Foucault — The Unconscious — Framing the 'Frost & Fire' episode as an imagined storyboard meeting, the chapter asks whether Finn's erotic dream of Flame Princess is a Freudian wish-fulfillment rising from his subconscious after he deliberately lies to provoke the Ice King-Flame Princess fight so the dream will return. Via Foucault's Care of the Self, it introduces Artemidorus's method of reading dreams for the real and moral consequences they portend, suggesting Finn's dream already warns him that his deception will cost him the relationship, with the Cosmic Owl whispering that he 'screwed up'. The writers conclude that sleeping and waking lives bleed into each other, and that Finn's refusal to read the warning leaves him burned: broken hearts, a torched Ice Kingdom, and the princess gone.
- ch. 27 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Gilbert Ryle — Personal Identity; The Ghost in the Machine — The chapter asks whether Marceline has lost Simon Petrikov forever now that he is the Ice King, and tests every criterion of personal identity - body, memories, beliefs, personality, soul - finding each one either something that changes over time without ending a person (Finn survives losing his arm, Jake his fear of vampires) or something shared that then explains nothing. Borrowing Ryle's deflation of the soul as just the way the brain works - like Lemongrab renaming and remaking the Candy Kingdom, killing it without touching a single building - the author concludes Simon and the Ice King are two different people sharing one piece of machinery, like two operating systems on one computer. The dark payoff: bringing Simon back permanently would delete the Ice King, and by the same reasoning our own past selves are equally gone, a 'thousand deaths' a day that the chapter offers as Marceline's consolation, with Death's line 'you're gonna be the Ice King' as the haunting exception.
- ch. 29 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Alan Turing, René Descartes, John Searle — The Turing Test; The Chinese Room; The Cogito — Arguing against the dogma that only organic beings can be conscious, the chapter defends BMO's aliveness and personhood against Finn and Jake's teasing and the contrast with servile Neptr. Using Pepperell's criteria of 'motivated meaning' and layered consciousness, it shows BMO changing her own batteries, escaping the giant bird, fearing the silent-contest 'doppelgangers', resisting the factory's personality wipe, and rehearsing personhood with Football in the mirror. Against Descartes's claim that no machine can truly use language and Searle's Chinese Room - reimagined as Gunter in a dungeon flipping response cards - the author sides with Turing: since we credit other humans with minds on conversation and behavior alone, refusing BMO the same credit is mere speciesism, and personhood finally rests on social recognition of another as a person.
- ch. 30 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — The chapter argues that what sets Adventure Time above generic sword-and-sorcery is that its stories are stories of play, from Card Wars duels to the pillow-fort world of 'Puhoy', where Finn lives out an entire alternate life with Rosalinen. Drawing on Huizinga's claim that play founds all culture, Gadamer's view that play is a presentation that reveals truth, and Fink's account of play as purposeless, world-creating magic, it shows Finn learning what a hero is by 'playing' the hero's role, BMO transforming a chicken into the noir suspect Lorraine, and Jake's imaginary lava genuinely burning Finn in 'Rainy Day Daydream'. Play-worlds like Ooo hold a mirror to the real one - Finn's experiments on the little people force Jake to confront what breaking up his relationship would mean - so make-believe turns out to be how we seriously learn who we are.
- ch. 31 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Judith Butler — Gender Performativity; Feminism — The chapter uses Adventure Time's gender play - Fionna and Cake, princesses holding nearly all political power in Ooo, Jake as terrified helicopter dad, Mannish Man's parody of manliness - to ask what being a man or woman really means. Following Judith Butler's Gender Trouble, it argues sex does not fix gender: the Lumpy Space King and Queen share one body, Flame King is a flame in a suit, and Butler's critique of the MIT 'master gene' experiment shows how the assumption that men and women are opposites smuggles cultural convention into science. Finn is read as performing masculinity - Billy worship, dungeon codes, the endless 'Dungeon Train' - caught in a crisis of masculinity between what society says a man is and who he is, with the ghost of Shoko in 'The Vault' and the accepted grass sword as steps toward a heroism that is his own.
- ch. 32 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Alan Turing — The Turing Test; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Staging a modified Turing Test in which the author interrogates BMO about Football, Bubble, her broken egg, her glitch and the Mo Co factory, the chapter asks whether her answers display human-like intelligence or merely a machine's 'pretend' intelligence. Beemo's evasions about emotion ('I felt like crying') become the pivot for asking whether anyone can define feeling beyond the words they were taught for it, since we are told as children that crying means sadness. Turing's conversational test is then weighed against our bias that a boxy Gameboy cannot really think - you are, the author notes, proof that arranged matter can love and feel - and the chapter closes on the ethics of the question: Princess Bubblegum's hacksaw shows that convenience is exactly the criterion we must never use to deny personhood, as slaveholders once did.
- ch. 33 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Epictetus — Stoicism; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Preferred Indifferents — Re-examining 'The Enchiridion!' trial by trial - the gnome illusions, the ogre whose dollar Finn steals and then returns, the dark mage's brain world, the wallop given the Key-per in devil pajamas - the chapter argues Finn wins the hero's handbook without being righteous: he is brave, tender and ingenious, but gullible, hasty and violent, slaying whatever he is told is evil and running from the gnome test. Epictetus's Stoic Enchiridion supplies the standard the show's book lacks: only virtue matters, wealth, fame and comfort are indifferents, and a real handbook teaches how to lose, age and admit mistakes, not just how to win, which is exactly what Billy's quit-heroism shows Ooo's greatest hero never learned. Because bravery without good judgment could as easily serve a Nazi, a terrorist or the Lich, Finn's lack of practical wisdom means the 'most righteous hero' in Ooo is an impetuous boy - proof of how morally broken the Land of Ooo is.
- ch. 35 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Socrates, Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche — Master and Slave Morality; The Unexamined Life; Justice in the Republic — Comparing Finn with Gilgamesh, Achilles, Cuchulainn and Beowulf, the chapter shows how deeply he belongs to the archaic heroic code: a warrior who loves combat, seeks glory in tough-guy contests, fights dirty like Odysseus, and is fiercely loyal to Jake, his friends and his community. Against this tradition, Finn's unprecedented willingness to help any stranger who cries for help and his refusal to kill the 'unaligned' ant mark the post-heroic morality that began when Socrates told Athenians to care for their souls rather than status and Plato designed a city serving the common good - the author explicitly frames this through Nietzsche's complaint that Greek philosophy derailed the healthy, competitive heroic values. The chapter sides with Finn and the self-sacrificing Lemonjohn over Achilles, concluding that the secret of the Enchiridion is doing whatever the common good requires, warrior or not.
- ch. 36 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Epictetus, Immanuel Kant — The Golden Mean; The Categorical Imperative; The Dichotomy of Control — The chapter assembles real-life versions of Finn's Enchiridion, starting with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: the Golden Mean locates each virtue between two vices, so true courage is knowing when to fight and when to run - cowardice and 'stupidteous' recklessness as deficiency and excess - a balance Finn's all-out bravery lacks. Epictetus's Stoic Handbook (which inspired the emperor Marcus Aurelius) teaches that happiness depends only on one's own reactions and that events are good or bad by how we take them, making it a manual even the chronically disappointed Ice King could use, while Christine de Pizan's book of chivalry prepares heroes for defeat and Erasmus's Handbook of the Christian Knight with Praise of Folly makes Finn and Jake's 'foolish' mercy look righteous. Finally Kant's Groundwork supplies duty for duty's sake: by the categorical imperative, Finn was entitled to steal the ogre's dollar only if, as an ogre who had swallowed Jake, he would accept the same theft from a hero.
- ch. 37 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Martha Nussbaum, John Stuart Mill, Immanuel Kant — Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Capabilities Approach — The chapter argues Finn is not yet a true hero but is on a quest to become one: against rule systems like Mill's greatest-happiness utilitarianism and Kantian respect for persons, virtue ethics asks not 'what should I do' but 'who should I be', and Aristotle's point that children lack fully developed practical reason explains why Finn's good intentions misfire - removing Donny exposes the house people to Why-wolves, and Penny's trick humiliates him in the City of Thieves. Martha Nussbaum's ideal of every person as free and of equal dignity grounds heroism in the common good, and her work on literature and popular culture explains how watching Finn's exaggerated choices trains our own moral judgment. Citing Franco and Zimbardo's psychology of real heroes - empathy, risk tolerance, persistence - and closing with Seneca's 'how nobly you live', it concludes that since Aristotelian virtue is a habit, anyone can start by admitting they suck at heroism and practicing, as Jake's advice puts it.
- ch. 38 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" **·** Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics; Moral Luck — Reading Finn's first season as a three-stage hero's journey - winning the Enchiridion on Mount Cragdor, being tested in 'Business Time', 'City of Thieves', 'Ocean of Fear' and 'Henchman', then doubly confirmed when Billy recognizes him - the chapter extracts a working handbook of heroism from his stumbles. Its lessons: heroism needs reason as much as courage (thinking through the gnome 'illusions', knocking himself unconscious to beat the Fear Feaster), plain luck plays a real and uneven part in saving Jake from the ogre, retribution should be temporary (the ogre's returned dollar), and heroes must check their sources (Penny's con). The deepest tension is that justice and compassion, instinct and reason, violence and non-violence must be perpetually balanced - Billy's nonviolent way becomes its own injustice when Finn medicates villagers without consent - so a real hero is simply someone who never stops trying to hold the balance.
- ch. 39 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Anime and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "What These Otaku Are Saying about" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Previews and Coming Attractions" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction argues that anime — from Akira, Ghost in the Shell, and Neon Genesis Evangelion to My Neighbor Totoro, Nausicaa, and Grave of the Fireflies — is not children's fare but stories about 'monsters, witches, robots, children, and spirits who grapple with questions of societal violence, ethics, morality, justice, heroism, identity, and the soul.' It frames the book's project as finding what lies beneath anime's visual signature of big eyes and giant robots, illustrating the tone with epigraphs from Wolf's Rain ('If life has no purpose, then you're already dead') and Princess Tutu on fate versus defiance. It closes with housekeeping: anime means Japan-originated animation for this book, Western name order will be used, and the contributing artists and industry supporters are thanked.
- ch. 7 "Accidental Anime" *(no index entry yet)* — A distributor's memoir, not a philosophical essay: Margo Zimmerman recounts falling into anime at Manga Entertainment via Ninja Scroll and Perfect Blue, and the art-versus-business balance of bringing a niche genre to Western audiences. Its philosophy-adjacent cases are concrete: otaku demanded authenticity over adaptation (fans rejected the Southern-accent dubbing of Mima's country mother in Perfect Blue, and the contested translation of End of Evangelion's final line 'kimochi warui' — 'How disgusting' vs 'I feel sick' — still divides viewers), and she credits anime's serious commentary on mythology, philosophy, nuclear power, and humanity with influencing Western storytelling, citing The Matrix's obvious debt to Ghost in the Shell. No taxonomy philosopher or concept is actually deployed.
- ch. 8 "Body" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Wave Goodbye from the Catbus" **·** The Ghost in the Machine; Embodiment (the lived body); The Extended Mind — Heinricy argues anime is the richest medium for posthuman theory because it shows bodies 'in a state of becoming' rather than as grotesque boundary violations: Miyazaki's Catbus and Totoro, Haku's dragon transformation and Chihiro's pig parents in Spirited Away, and the cursed pig-headed aviator of Porco Rosso all treat morphing bodies as possibility, not horror. She sorts anime posthumanism into two valences: a 'Ghost in the Machine' dream of consciousness leaving the body altogether (Motoko merging with the net in Ghost in the Shell), which she rebuts via N. Katherine Hayles's point that consciousness is embodied and would change with any new body, and hybrid configurations like mecha (Gundam, Robotech) where body and machine drive each other. Following Donna Haraway, she contends we are all already cyborgs — vaccines, engineered food, treated water — and credits Japan's nuclear history (via Susan Napier) and its shape-shifting folklore for why anime embraces rather than fears the transformed body.
- ch. 10 "Looking Inwards" **·** The Male Gaze; Objectification; Feminism — Barber, Bryce, and Davis test Donna Haraway's emancipatory cyborg thesis against Gunslinger Girl, where the Social Welfare Agency 'adopts' orphaned and abused girls (Henrietta, Rico, Triela, Elsa, Claes), rebuilds their bodies as cybernetic weapons, and drug-conditions them into loyal assassins paired with male handlers. They argue the series realizes none of Haraway's post-gender potential: conditioning erodes memory and autonomy (Rico coolly shoots the porter Emilio who befriended her; Elsa murders her handler Lauro and kills herself; Triela suffers pointless menstrual cramps in a wombless body), while the girls' kawaii styling, teddy bears, and school uniforms make them objects of the male gaze whose cuteness disguises lethal power. The cyborgs' victimization ultimately reinforces traditional gender hierarchy and mirrors conformity-pressured Japanese youth, so the cyborg has 'regressed' from the autonomous heroines of Ghost in the Shell or Battle Angel Alita.
- ch. 11 "The Transforming Body" **·** Martin Heidegger — Embodiment (the lived body); Mind–Body Dualism; Dasein (being-there); The Extended Mind — McBlane reads Oshii's Ghost in the Shell as staging the collision between a humanist framework — Cartesian ghost-in-shell dualism where consciousness is the seat of identity — and a posthuman 'mindbody' of distributed cognition in which the body is an informational circuit extending into the net, so a data body is still a body. Motoko's crisis (is the real me the organic brain, the ghost, or nothing?) deepens through the hacked garbage-truck man ('There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost') and resolves only in her fusion with the Puppet Master, whose line 'Your effort to remain what you are is what limits you' enacts the shift from one ghost to multiple, distributed subjectivities ending in a little girl's body with 'The net is vast.' Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world supply the claim that access to Being expands beyond the human into technological and informational modes, while the film's angelic transcendence imagery shows how residual humanist mind-body splits persist even in a posthuman story.
- ch. 12 "Mind" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Is Everybody Disembodied (or, Have We Always Been Posthuman Beings )" **·** René Descartes, John Searle, Alan Turing, Aristotle, Plutarch, Heraclitus, Augustine of Hippo, Daniel Dennett — Personal Identity; The Cogito; Mind–Body Dualism; Ship of Theseus — Stevens uses the film's closing voice-over 'I am Tetsuo' in Otomo's Akira to run the classic identity-and-mind problems: Heraclitus's river and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus ask whether the grotesquely transformed, Akira-absorbed Tetsuo is still the same person, while Descartes's cogito — riffed as 'cogito ergo Tetsuo' — Turing's Test, and Searle's Chinese Room test whether a voice that seems to think proves a thinker behind it (syntax is not yet shown sufficient for semantics, though Edwin Hutchins's distributed cognition reads the Room from the inside out). Weighing embodiment (Pinker's brain-makes-mind, Dennett's self as a 'center of narrative gravity') against disembodiment (Akira levelling Neo-Tokyo from nothing but cryogenically stored remains; Tetsuo's matter teleportation), he concludes through the problem of representation — every utterance is re-presented, as in Augustine's guilty tears over Dido — that we always treat semblances of thinkers as thinkers, so we may have always been decentered, re-presented, posthuman beings no different from Tetsuo and Akira.
- ch. 14 "Questioning the Question" **·** William James, Blaise Pascal — The Will to Believe; Pascal's Wager; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Hartung takes Ross's snapping reply to Armitage's repeated 'Why are you helping me?' in Armitage the Third: Poly-Matrix as a misreading: she wants a practical reason for his choice, not theoretical evidence, and since no evidence can prove an android is a person, William James's 'Will to Believe' applies — Ross's belief in her moral standing is a live, forced, and momentous genuine option (suspending judgment means she is scrapped, and losing her means losing a possible life together), so his passions may legitimately decide. He contrasts this with evidentialist cases where suspending judgment is right (the shuttle company skipping inspection; Dr. Asakura's silicon-based-life hypothesis) and with Pascal's Wager, reading Mars's church-empty, hedonistic culture of sex-tourism Seconds as one that denies genuine options and so kills Thirds. The attached original screenplay 'Eye Am,' a sequel to Magnetic Rose, extends the theme as salvage officer Nadine Beckner is lured by the AI Eva/Sam impersonating her dead husband Heintz, with Schrodinger-style observer-affected reality deciding which version becomes real.
- ch. 15 "Spirit" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "In the Palm of Your Hand" *(no index entry yet)* — Callis reads Spirited Away as Miyazaki's bid to make audiences feel rather than doctrinally learn Shinto, deploying Thomas Kasulis's distinction between existential Shinto (awe before kami: Chihiro's soot-sprite rescue, cleansing the trash-choked River God, makoto no kokoro purity) and essentialist Shinto (State Shinto's war-era nationalism, visually evoked by the abandoned 1940s train station and the train that haunts the whole film). She argues the drive into the spirit world is a compressed visual history of Shinto — folk shrines, Buddhist guardian statues, torii — and that Chihiro's stolen and recovered name enacts Japan's need to remember its traditions without forgetting how they were abused, supported by Miyazaki's own quotes on rural solstice bath rituals and Tarkovsky-style nostalgia. The three endings (Zeniba's 'Nothing that happens is ever forgotten' vs the Disney dub's memory-will-return line, and Miyazaki's preferred solo train ride) all say the same: the kami spark, like Thich Nhat Hanh's ancestors in the palm of the hand, is carried forward.
- ch. 17 "Gay Angels, Female Cardinals, and Bishōnen Popes" **·** Immanuel Kant, Augustine of Hippo — Phenomena and Noumena; Moral Relativism; The Two Cities — Barkman argues that anime's Christian imagery — the legendary Santa on a cross, Earthian's gay angel lovers, Trinity Blood's bishonen pope and female cardinal, Evangelion's hostile Angels — encodes Japanese religious pluralism rather than orthodox Christianity. He lays out the pluralist position (following Kant's phenomena/noumena distinction and John Hick: Ultimate Reality is only equivocally describable, so doctrine matters less than spiritual mood), contrasts it with exclusivism and inclusivism, and charges pluralism with self-undermining intolerance, then traces Japan's historical demonization of Christianity from the 1637 Shimabara massacre (Ninja Resurrection, Samurai Champloo) to Eva's alien invaders, with Armageddon imagery fueled by the atomic bombs. Because Shinto-Buddhist-Daoist anti-realism dissolves fixed categories, anime dissolves good and evil (Chrno Crusade's I Ching balance) and gender itself, gravitating to the symbol-rich 'jungle' of Catholicism (C.S. Lewis's phrase) — and where Trinity Blood lets some vampires be righteous, Augustine's City of God marks the one nearly orthodox note.
- ch. 18 "The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back" **·** Immanuel Kant — Consequentialism; Humanity as an End in Itself; Anthropocentrism — Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy. Because she respects the jungle and the sentient Ohmu rather than viewing nature anthropocentrically as a plague to burn, she discovers the plants are purifying the war-poisoned earth — the knowledge that saves everyone and proves Kushana's conquering approach self-defeating even on its own terms.
- ch. 19 "Conflict" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Freeing Clausewitz’s Soul from Gravity" **·** Michael Walzer — Just War Theory — Melancon tests Just War Theory against Gundam's One Year War: Gihren Zabi's 'Sieg Zeon' funeral oration and Char Aznable's rhetoric show how the vague criterion of comparative justice lets a militarist regime dress aggression — the Three Seconds of Declaration gassing of colonies, Operation British's colony drop on Earth — in just-war language. On the conduct side, Ramba Ral's troops spare civilians and differentiate child targets on White Base, yet Zeon's still-unjust ad bellum position cannot be rehabilitated; and asking whether WMDs are inherently immoral, he uses Anavel Gato's nuclear strike on the Federation fleet review (Operation Stardust) — discriminating, proportional, militarily necessary — to argue weapons are amoral tools judged only by Walzer-style jus in bello criteria. Clausewitz resolves the theory's usefulness: war's inner tendency toward the absolute must stay nested within political goals, and Zeon's drift from fighting for independence into conquering and governing Earth shows exactly how a war that abandons just-war limits loses sight of what victory even is.
- ch. 21 "Redemption and Hope for the Future" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Peters applies Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of courage — the mean between confidence and fear, shown only in facing an honorable death in war for a noble motive — to Colin MacLeod's two-thousand-year hunt for Marcus Octavius, the Immortal Roman who killed his wife Moya, in Highlander: The Search for Vengeance. Because MacLeod fights from pain and rage, 'like wild beasts,' and secretly seeks death as refuge from grief ('to seek death as a refuge from poverty, or love... is not the act of a brave man'), Aristotle would judge him a coward despite his fearlessness — Amergan the spirit guide diagnoses him the same way. Redemption comes only when Dahlia and the villagers threatened by Marcus's new Rome give him a noble cause and hopefulness: he becomes their general, fights with discipline instead of rage, and turns Marcus's own quickening to destroying the virus, illustrating the chapter's closing thought that for an Immortal dying is easy and living courageously is hard.
- ch. 22 "Don’t Be a Vegeta" **·** Adam Smith — The Invisible Hand; Social Darwinism — Argues that shonen fighting anime stage a choice between Adam Smith's and Darwin's models of competition: Zoro hunting Mihawk in One Piece, Goku's technique-by-technique training, and Rock Lee's specialization show competition improving people within the limits of a human excellence, while Cell's absorbing evolutions, the Super Saiyan transformations, and Ichigo's risky hollowification represent limitless 'leveling up' that changes what you are. The chapter concludes that the Darwinian win-at-all-costs model produces the perpetually dissatisfied Vegeta, and that framing competition around being a certain kind of person (a great swordsman, not just a winner) gives life a completable aim — while conceding that Darwinians rightly warn our picture of the 'normal human' has unjustly cast off jinchūriki like Naruto and Gaara and Devil Fruit users like Luffy.
- ch. 23 "Heroes" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Alchemic Heroism" **·** Yin and Yang; Buddhism — Reads Edward and Alphonse Elric as a single composite 'alchemic hero' who fuses Japanese heroic archetypes: the dual-hero rooted in the Izanami-Izanagi creation myth and yin-yang complementarity (brash yang Ed, calm yin Al whose armored body actually fights better), the student hero forged by Izumi Curtis's brutal island training, and the wandering redemption seeker atoning for the forbidden attempt to resurrect their mother. It argues that the sacrifice built into this fusion — Al's lost senses, puberty, and body — mirrors Japan's own cultural alchemy of absorbing Buddhism, Confucianism, and yin-yang thought while retaining a coherent national identity.
- ch. 25 "The Sacrificial Lamb" **·** Martin Heidegger, Theodor Adorno, Plato — The Question Concerning Technology; Theory of Forms — Argues Astro Boy re-enacts the sacrificial logic of the atomic age: Atomu is the nuclear-powered copy of the dead Tobio, born from Dr. Tenma's refusal to accept mortality, and his repeated self-sacrifice for humans who discard him (as in 'Save the Classmate,' where the rescued boys' parents still want him removed) shows him functioning as Heidegger's 'standing-reserve' — an object valued only as stored power, with humans themselves next in line. Drawing on Plato's Republic anxiety over originals and copies, Adorno and Horkheimer's dialectic of enlightenment, and Rey Chow's account of mimesis as the sign left by sacrifice, the chapter reads the series as mourning an innocence that became impossible after Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
- ch. 26 "The Aftermath of Tragedy" **·** Aristotle — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Potentiality and Actuality — Argues that Grave of the Fireflies works as a critique of anime's child-hero convention: Seita acts exactly like a plucky anime protagonist when he defies his not-actually-evil aunt, strikes out on his own with Setsuko, ignores the farmer's advice to apologize and return, and demands a quick fix from the doctor — but these 'heroic' choices kill them both, because he lacks the developed capacity to reason. Against the medieval 'child as little adult' picture that most anime (Dragon Ball, Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!) romanticizes, the chapter deploys Aristotle's view of children as unfinished beings who cannot yet reason or achieve happiness, concluding the film is a cautionary tale about the years of nurture and guidance real children need.
- ch. 27 "Devils" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Equivalent Exchange" **·** John Locke, Karl Marx, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Labor Theory of Property; Alienation; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Reads alchemy's law of equivalent exchange as a parable of capitalism: Locke's labor-mixing argument explains how hours of a life become property and why money is 'distilled life'; Aristotle's attack on limitless wealth-getting (the Midas problem) and Aquinas's capital vices explain how pursuing money for its own sake brings the homunculi — Greed, Pride, and the Sloth the Elric brothers' forbidden act produced — into the world. Marx's 1844 Manuscripts supply the punchline that money performs 'human alchemy' on people, buying their time, esteem, and bodies the way red stones are made from sacrificed humans, so the chapter concludes that capital, like the Philosopher's Stone, profits only by consuming lives and that markets must be held to a promise of fairness and care beyond mere exchange.
- ch. 29 "Textually Transmitted Disease" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Objectification — Traces hentai from Hokusai's 'Diver and Two Octopi' through the 1920s eroguro journals to the Lolita Anime and Cream Lemon OVAs, then asks whether even this extreme material has value as fantasy. The chapter frames the media-effects debate with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis (revived by Feshbach and tentatively supported by Milton Diamond's finding that Japanese rape rates fell as pornography spread) against Plato's Republic worry that sensational works license irrationality (updated by the Disinhibition, Desensitization, and Cultivation theories), and concludes that hentai's real harm is attitudinal rather than behavioral: its ritual 'breaking' of strong women and sex-as-something-done-to-passive-girls cultivates misogyny and a dehumanizing view of sex.
- ch. 30 "18 - The Devil Within Sara Livingston" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Future Perfect" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "Who Wants to Be Human Anyway" **·** Gilbert Ryle, René Descartes — The Ghost in the Machine; Atman and Brahman; Mind–Body Dualism — Reads Kenji Kawai's thrice-repeated minyo 'Ghost theme' as the key to Major Kusanagi's quest in Ghost in the Shell and Innocence: each richer orchestration tracks her progress from manufactured shell, through the diving-scene worry that only others' treatment makes her human, to merging with the Puppet Master. Using Koestler's holons — individuals preserved while functioning within an evolving whole — and his view of consciousness as emergent (itself a rejection of both Descartes's immaterial soul and Ryle's dismissal of the 'ghost in the machine'), the chapter argues Oshii first celebrates the Major's Atman-like self-transcendence, then subverts Koestler in Innocence by making machines human: the ghost-dubbed gynoids act as a voiceless pack while the Major, still recognizably herself, aids Batou from the net — and Kawai's music literally gives the dolls a voice.
- ch. 33 "Cyborg Goddess" **·** Gilbert Ryle, René Descartes, Plato — The Ghost in the Machine; Mind–Body Dualism; Allegory of the Cave — Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.
- ch. 34 "One Last Anguished Existential Scream" **·** Martin Heidegger — The They-Self (das Man); Authenticity; Free Will vs Determinism — Argues Neon Genesis Evangelion and Akira dramatize a justified anxiety about humanity's evolutionary future: SEELE's Human Instrumentality Project — dissolving everyone into the Sea of LCL because separate, mutually harming individuals have 'run the course' of their evolution — is Heideggerian anxiety (the objectless unease that breaks us out of 'the They') curdled, via Mary Midgley's 'fatalism,' into the belief that genes, Moore's Law, or 'the Market' leave no room for human choice. Akira's Numbered Children, who sacrifice themselves to remove Tetsuo and save Kaneda, model the responsible alternative: accepting that the power is coming, screaming about it, and still choosing how humanity faces it rather than abdicating to fate.
- ch. 35 "Anime and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "ALTERNATE ENDING" *(no index entry yet)* — A closing personal essay arguing that anime's defining gift is the genuinely unexpected — a robot sprouting from Naota's forehead bump in Fooly Cooly, Berserk's catastrophic finale, Samurai Champloo's Edo-meets-hip-hop fusion, Paprika's dream parade — which jolts viewers into noticing and rethinking their expectations, the very opening that philosophic inquiry requires. It also credits anime's sincere, two-way engagement with its audience (the cast-and-crew interviews on DVD extras that won the author over) for the genre's ongoing, unpredictable evolution.
- ch. 37 "Credits" *(notes)*

## Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Baseball and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Foreword" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "Pre-Game Warm-up" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "First Inning - Hometown Heroes" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Rounding Third and Heading Home" *(no index entry yet)* — Joe Kraus uses Gaston Bachelard's Poetics of Space to read baseball's 'home': the batter begins at home yet must leave it, face the pitcher's threat, and return to make scoring meaningful, which is Bachelard's dialectic of shelter versus threat (with Joseph Campbell's monomyth alongside). Freud's uncanny (unheimlich, un-home-like) explains why home plate is both inviting and demoralizing. Bachelard's 'well-determined centers of revery' and Benedict Anderson's shared-news account of nationhood then explain ballparks as communal homes, from Wrigleyville to 'Cardinal Nation' in Quincy, Illinois, and why the Dodgers leaving Brooklyn felt like losing a home.
- ch. 11 "The Obligation to Play Baseball" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle — Horan and Solomon examine the 2001-02 contraction fight in which Judge Harry Crump ordered the Minnesota Twins to honor their Metrodome lease and play the 2002 season. They argue the Minnesota courts smuggled Bentham-Mill utilitarian reasoning about the public good into contract law, which normally awards only money damages, because baseball's antitrust exemption (from Justice Holmes's 1922 ruling through Justice Blackmun's 1972 opinion) had always treated the game as more than a business. Having long profited from special treatment, the owners lost when Bud Selig's plan to eliminate the Twins collided with the same 'greatest good for the greatest number' logic.
- ch. 12 "Second Inning - You Gotta Believe!" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" **·** Blaise Pascal, William James — Pascal's Wager; Faith and Reason; The Will to Believe — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- ch. 14 "Kierkegaard Lays It Down" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Aristotle, G.W.F. Hegel, Seneca — Teleological Suspension of the Ethical; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Stoicism; Geist (World Spirit) — Willie Young uses the sacrifice bunt (Derek Jeter's perfect one versus Placido Polanco's failed one) to test philosophical accounts of sacrifice. Aristotle treats bunting for teammates as friendship and civic virtue in the polis, while Seneca's Stoic sacrifices only to exercise virtue itself, detached from particular friends and refusing retaliation for hit batters. Hegel's modern ideal of self-renunciation makes the player a cog in the team machine (the Big Red Machine), obeying the manager's calculations; against this, Kierkegaard's Abraham, whose absolute duty to God is 'higher than the universal' through infinite resignation, exposes baseball's mechanical, manager-ordered sacrifice and asks whether the game trains obedient citizens who sacrifice as they are told.
- ch. 15 "Third Inning - The Umpire’s New Clothes" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "The Ambiguous Consolations of Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Ted Cohen shows that 'ties go to the runner' is no convention but follows from Rule 6.05(j) (the runner is out only if tagged before he touches first), then discovers that Rule 7.08(e) contradicts 6.05(j) once 6.09(a) makes a batter who hits a fair ball a runner: on a tie at first the rules say both out and safe. His letters to the National League rules committee get a polite brush-off ('there never are any ties'), and the essay meditates on how players barely know the rules (the 2000 World Series third-strike misplay, cricket's time-wasting law, the spitball rule's gaps) and how rules written 'by journeymen lawyers' charm yet fail. Philosophy's consolation is ambiguous: knowing the rules cost him his teammates' respect, who 'knew the game in some other way.'
- ch. 17 "The Integrity of the Game" *(no index entry yet)* — J.S. Russell argues umpires have far more discretion than 'rules are all an umpire has to work with' allows. Via J.L. Austin's performative utterances, a call both creates the out and reports a witnessed event, so it can be false; hence unwitnessed or deceived calls (Ken Burkhart's 1970 World Series missed tag, phantom tags, Bernardo Carbo never touching the plate) should be reviewable to prevent an 'anti-game.' Via Ronald Dworkin's law-as-integrity he then defends Lee MacPhail's reinstatement of George Brett's pine-tar home run and umpire Wes Curry's 1887 interference ruling through a 'first principle of games adjudication': interpret rules to preserve the lusory goal and the excellences the game tests, as umpires' de facto strike-zone management has held league batting averages near .260 for a century.
- ch. 18 "Fourth Inning - Fair or Foul" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Kant, Aristotle, and the Cheater" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Socrates — The Categorical Imperative; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Socratic Method (elenchus) — Answering Cal Ripken's Socratic question 'What is cheating?' (raised by Sammy Sosa's corked bat and Gaylord Perry's spitball), Randolph Feezell stages a dialogue between Abbey's Kantian absolutism, Trev's traditionalism, and Ron's win-at-all-costs realism. Kant's categorical imperative grounds the absolutist: intending to break a rule to gain an edge is making yourself an arbitrary exception to rules that bind all players equally. Aristotle's virtue ethics then lets the traditionalist say that some strategic rule-breaking belongs to a sport's 'prescriptive atmosphere' (stealing signs, the balk pickoff, catching framing), since honesty and courage are means between excess and defect guided by judgment rather than exceptionless rules, while corking a bat stays cheating because it defies the tradition and hides from umpires.
- ch. 20 "Five Questions about Good Sportsmanship" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Aquinas, Augustine of Hippo — The Categorical Imperative — Mark Hamilton asks whether there is lying in baseball (riffing on Jimmy Dugan's 'There's no crying in baseball') and sorts plays of deception by their target. Kant's absolute duty of truthfulness proves too broad for the hidden ball trick, Omar Vizquel's decoys, and faking a tag to fool Manny Ramirez: Aquinas's taxonomy of officious, jocose, and mischievous lies (with Bonhoeffer's situational truth-telling) shows these are jocose falsehoods in an agreed artificial contest, not immoral lies. But deception aimed at umpires is mischievous and immoral, as when Barry Bonds sells a trapped ball as a catch or runners cut bases in the illegal double squeeze; his five questions conclude that tricking opponents is strategy while tricking the officials destroys character and sport.
- ch. 21 "Fifth Inning - Baseball and America" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "Our Big, Fat, Greek Democracy" **·** Socrates, Adam Smith, Friedrich Nietzsche — Democracy; The Invisible Hand; The Unexamined Life — Eric Bronson reads the brawling 1977-78 'Bronx Zoo' Yankees (Steinbrenner firing Billy Martin five times, Martin dragging Reggie Jackson off the field in Fenway, Jackson's dugout charge and defiant bunt) as an argument that dissent is good for democracy. Through Alexis de Tocqueville's warnings about majority conformity and democratic leveling (Nietzsche's herd mentality), he argues America needs gadflies like Socrates condemned by Athens for 'creating tension' and MLK's nonviolent troublemakers, while Adam Smith's invisible hand shows the Yankees' internal self-interest and conflict still produced championships, unlike the harmonious 1979 'We Are Family' Pirates. Dysfunctional discord, like free speech, keeps teams and democracies from going stagnant.
- ch. 23 "America’s Game" **·** Richard Rorty, Alasdair MacIntyre, Bernard Williams — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Communitarianism — William Morgan answers Richard Rorty's charge that American pop culture breeds only militaristic chauvinism by pointing to baseball's moral self-story: played for love of the game (Whitman) rather than market value. Using MacIntyre's notion of a practice's internal goods, he argues baseball's excellences and fair play are shared, socially constructed goods that resist commodification; through Annette Baier's ethics of trust and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' (saving your wife because she is your wife), the home team extends familial trust into a public moral community. Hence the moral outrage of 'Say it ain't so, Joe' after the 1919 Black Sox scandal and 'Say It Ain't So Sammy' after Sosa's corked bat: fans demand that players justify themselves to the community whose common good the game embodies.
- ch. 24 "Sixth Inning - Where Have You Gone, Jackie Robinson" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 25 "Crossing the Color Line" **·** Herbert Spencer — Social Darwinism — The Rucks argue that Herbert Spencer's Social Darwinism supplied the ideological justification for baseball's color line — blacks were deemed genetically unfit for the game — and that the Negro Leagues disproved it. Rube Foster's Negro National League, and especially Pittsburgh's Homestead Grays and Pittsburgh Crawfords (Cum Posey, Josh Gibson, Satchel Paige, Cool Papa Bell), displayed black organizational skill and on-field excellence, with Negro League teams beating white major leaguers in barnstorming play. Drawing on Darwin's actual account of cultural evolution and Franz Boas's environmental anthropology, the chapter holds that institutions, training infrastructure, and environment — not genes — explain athletic success, as Jackie Robinson's 1947 crossing of the color line and the later rise of Latin stars like Roberto Clemente confirm.
- ch. 26 "The Gift of Baseball" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Cornel West, bell hooks — Ressentiment; Cultural Hegemony — McDaniels reads the Negro Leagues through Nietzsche's account of resentment as revolt and Cornel West's tragic philosophy of resistance: excluded from the white majors after Cap Anson's 1887 stand against George Stovey, black players converted resentment into counter-narratives of excellence, with Satchel Paige, Josh Gibson, and Buck O'Neil showboating and clowning in the tradition of plantation dance, gallows humor, and the blues. The call-and-response sermon scene from The Bingo Long Traveling All-Stars & Motor Kings — Bingo Long on the mound answered by the crowd like a black church congregation — shows performance as ritual that sustains community, while bell hooks's 'absence of presence' frames remembering as resistance to hegemonic definitions of race. The chapter closes with the author's grandfather, for whom Robinson, Aaron, Mays, and Paige proved with every pitch 'We're American Too.'
- ch. 27 "Seventh Inning - The Japanese National Pastime" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Ballparks, Dojos, and Other Places of Enlightenment" **·** The Buddha — Zen Buddhism; Buddhism — Bassham argues that the core advice of hitting instructors like Ted Williams ('get a good ball to hit') and Charley Lau ('tension is the enemy') echoes Zen Buddhist principles, walking through patience, relaxation, self-knowledge, visualization (Reggie Jackson, Willie Stargell, Barry Bonds's on-deck imagery), practice, Bruce Lee-style kime concentration, and mushin or no-mind. Mickey Mantle going 0-for-30 after over-thinking Ted Williams's hitting tips, and Tony Gwynn's 'see the ball and react,' show how conscious analysis interferes with the muscle memory a half-second fastball demands. If kendo is practiced in a dojo — a 'place of enlightenment' — he concludes, ballparks and batting cages may be dojos too, with the caveat that Cobb, Ruth, and Mantle hardly model egoless humility.
- ch. 29 "What’s Wrong with Generalization" **·** The Buddha, Confucius — Zen Buddhism; Buddhism — Brannigan uses Japanese baseball to ask what is wrong with cultural generalization. He presents the Bushido case — samurai-style self-denial, absolute loyalty (Kawakami's Yomiuri Giants), Suisha Tobita's 'training of death,' resolve (konjo), team harmony (wa), and a relational self grounded in Buddhism's no-self and Confucian identity-through-relationships — then tests it against counter-evidence: Sadaharu Oh's flamingo swing owed as much to individual talent and Hiroshi Arakawa's unconventional kendo-and-aikido coaching as to sensei imitation, the 'new breed' (Ochiai, Egawa) flouts the old ways, and William Kelly's 'Whiting problem' warns against polarizing Japanese and American baseball. The chapter's 'three strikes' against the label 'Japanese baseball' conclude that generalizations become dangerous when treated as monolithic nets cast over an entire culture.
- ch. 30 "Eighth Inning - Behind in the Count" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "Numbers as Players" **·** Thomas Kuhn, Michel Foucault — Power/Knowledge — Bennett and Martin argue that the statistics baseball fans treat as objective truth embody far more chance and convention than fans realize. Statistical theory shows luck explains roughly half the spread in 2002 batting averages (Bonds's .370 versus Larry Walker; the 2003 Ramirez–Mueller race decided by one at bat), and Jim Albert's simulation of 1,000 seasons shows about four of five World Series are not won by the most talented team. Drawing on Thomas Kuhn's history of scientific quantification and Theodore Porter's Foucauldian point that numbers 'have agency' and exercise power, they show statistics also act on the game — shaping drafting, salaries, and Hall of Fame election — so Schroeder's stats to Charlie Brown are both indispensable and misleading.
- ch. 32 "Softball The Good Is the Enemy of the Best" **·** Iris Marion Young, Simone de Beauvoir — Feminism; Woman as the Other; Embodiment (the lived body) — Heaphy asks whether softball limits women's potential to be equals on the baseball diamond, using feminist philosophy to explain why women are steered to the 'soft' game. Judith Williamson's analysis of women in mass culture and Simone de Beauvoir's woman-as-invisible-Other explain why female players — the AAGPBL's skirts and charm school, Toni Stone and Mamie Johnson in the Negro Leagues, Ila Borders in the minors — are covered as women first and ballplayers second. Iris Marion Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl' supplies the phenomenology: women throw differently not from anatomy but from experiencing the body as a burden, a socially produced self-fulfilling prophecy. Softball, 'the good,' becomes the enemy of the best — women playing hardball — by letting society postpone hard questions about gender.
- ch. 33 "Ninth Inning - Under Pressure" *(front)*
- ch. 34 "The Moral and Aesthetic Superiority of Baseball" **·** John Searle — Kretchmar asks whether the intentional walk of sluggers like Barry Bonds (or Casey at the Bat) is an unfair cop-out. Building an account of games as 'artificial tests' (via Bernard Suits and John Searle's treatment of conventions like 'hello'), he tests the analogy with basketball stalling and finds it fails: walking Bonds shifts rather than avoids the defensive test (the fielding team still owes all its outs), team games legitimately run away from stars as basketball double-teams Shaq, and fans gain new drama — Jeff Kent batting with the tying run after Bonds's walk. He concludes that event-regulated games like baseball, which cannot be shortened, enjoy a moral and aesthetic superiority over time-regulated games, whose endings breed stalling and clock-killing fouls.
- ch. 35 "Last Pitch" **·** Socrates, Plato — Socratic Method (elenchus); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Allegory of the Cave; The Unexamined Life — Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.
- ch. 36 "Post-Game - Press Conference" *(front)*
- ch. 37 "19b" **·** Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Utilitarianism — A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.
- ch. 38 "20b" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, Adam Smith — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; The Invisible Hand — A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.
- ch. 39 "21b" **·** William James — The Will to Believe — A paired metaphysics debate on whether superstition helps performance. Steven Streeter argues yes: baseball's mystery-rich outcomes breed ritual (Sparky Anderson refusing to step on foul lines, Wade Boggs's chicken, Nomar Garciaparra's glove taps), whose invisible forces — like black holes — can be inferred from their measurable effects on attention, preparation, and focus, with William James's belief-makes-reality as the capstone. Neil Feit counters no: on the counterfactual account of helping, a player cured of superstition would perform the same since his athletic ability is untouched, routines that aid concentration need involve no magical belief, and the burden of proof lies with the believer.
- ch. 40 "22b" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — A paired legal-philosophy debate on whether steroids should be banned. Michael McGrath argues yes from Kant: PED use cannot be universalized and 'the ends do not justify the means,' so the Ken Caminiti, Mark McGwire, and José Canseco confessions stain America's pastime, whose stars are role models and whose users risk devastating health effects — down to wrestler Davey Boy Smith's fatal steroid-related heart attack. Simon Eassom replies no by reframing drugs as Performance Enhancing Technologies: rules merely define the game, enhancers (unlike bat-cannons or netted catcher's gloves) do not de-skill baseball, and banning them because we dislike them is a matter of taste — of aesthetics, not ethics.
- ch. 41 "23b" *(no index entry yet)* — A paired aesthetics debate over the best baseball movie. Vincent Toscano picks The Natural: Robert Redford's Roy Hobbs enacts fall and redemption, Barry Levinson's halo-lit amber cinematography gives the film its mythic beauty, and its Reagan-era warmth answered America's post-sixties malaise. Larry Raful counters with It Happens Every Spring: the best baseball film lets the common man — Ray Milland's chemistry teacher armed with a wood-repelling mystery juice — dream himself into the Show, and he notes we cheer fictional cheating on screen while demanding that the real game stay pure.
- ch. 42 "24b" **·** Socrates — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — A paired philosophy-of-education debate on whether baseball players were better role models then or now. Edward Sullivan answers 'then' from lived memory: Ted Williams's Korean War service and his 1966 Hall of Fame induction speech demanding Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson be enshrined, and Jackie Robinson enduring Jim Crow spring training under Branch Rickey's pact of 'guts enough not to fight back.' Graham Harman answers 'now,' turning Socrates's Apology complaint that his most dangerous accusers are those safely dead into a diagnosis of nostalgia: the past buried Ty Cobb's and Cap Anson's racism, the Black Sox, and Hal Chase, while today's game is more racially open, physically dedicated, and union-protected.
